# Embeddings: Words as Coordinates {#sec-embeddings}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** Every number and every code output on this page
was produced by running the code shown, with `gensim` 4.4, `scikit-learn`
1.9 and NumPy 2.5 on Python 3.12. The skip-gram, analogy and subword
explorers are interactive.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- explain the distributional hypothesis and turn it into a matrix, then into coordinates;
- reweight co-occurrence counts with PPMI: the score for how much more often two words land together than chance predicts;
- compress the result with truncated SVD — the method that keeps a table's strongest patterns and drops the rest — and say what each step fixes;
- write skip-gram with negative sampling from scratch and explain it as a logistic regression;
- choose between word2vec, GloVe, fastText and doc2vec for a stated problem, and defend it;
- diagnose three defects of the space: vectors sharing a common direction (anisotropy), a vector recording frequency as much as meaning, and cosine failing to separate "mentioned together" from "means the same thing";
- state precisely what a static embedding cannot do, which is exactly what @sec-transformers exists to fix.

## The problem, in one sentence

@sec-text-as-data ended in an uncomfortable place. Document vectors worked,
but one-hot word vectors shared no similarity between words at all.

Every word was a one-hot column, so `pump`, `pumps` and `impeller` were three
mutually orthogonal directions — each as unrelated to the others as `pump` is
to `Wednesday`. Cosine similarity between any two distinct words was exactly
zero. By construction. Always.

A good representation should be able to tell three relations apart:
morphological closeness like `pump`–`pumps`, semantic or functional closeness
like `pump`–`impeller`, and unrelatedness like `pump`–`Wednesday`.

How bad is that, really? Bad enough that the model cannot generalise across
*word forms* at all. Suppose your training data contains *the pump failed*
and your test data contains *the pumps failed*. The two sentences do share
`the` and `failed`, so something transfers — but everything the model learned
about `pump` specifically is filed under a coordinate the second sentence never
touches.

::: {#gloss-embedding .column-margin .term-gloss}
**embedding** — a short list of numbers standing in for a word, arranged
so that words used in similar ways sit close together. Think of it as
giving every word a set of map coordinates. [↩](#term-embedding){.term-back}
:::

This chapter fixes exactly that, and the whole fix is one idea: instead of
treating every word as its own axis, we place all words in one shared
coordinate system. In linear-algebra terms that means
[replacing the identity matrix with a learned one]{.hl}.

Instead of giving each word its own axis, give it a short list of numbers —
100 of them, or 300 — positioned so that words used in similar ways end up
near each other. That list is an [embedding]{.hl}.

**What we will look at.** We will build the space twice. First by counting,
because that version can be checked by hand and every number is small enough
to print. Then by predicting, which is word2vec — and we will write it from
scratch, gradients included, before showing that the two routes were the same
route all along. After that: what the space is good at, the three defects it
hides, and the one thing it cannot do at all, which is exactly what
@sec-transformers exists to fix.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Deep dive: the statistician's framing

One-hot encoding is a saturated model with one parameter per category and no
pooling. An [embedding](#gloss-embedding){#term-embedding .term-ref} is the
same model with a low-rank constraint, which is a form of partial pooling.
Words that behave alike are forced to share parameters, and that sharing *is*
the generalisation.
:::

## The distributional hypothesis

> *"You shall know a word by the company it keeps."* — J.R. Firth, 1957
> [@firth1957synopsis]

Firth was making a point about linguistic method; Zellig Harris had already
made the operational version of it [@harris1954distributional]. The claim is
that a substantial amount of semantic and functional information about a word
can be recovered from the distribution of contexts it appears in.

Put concretely: if two words keep appearing in the same slots —
`the ___ failed`, `replaced the ___`, `___ pressure dropped` — then their uses
are systematically similar.

Is that true? Not quite, and it is worth being clear that it is a bet rather
than a theorem. It works extraordinarily well for topical and functional
similarity. It fails for antonyms, because *hot* and *cold* keep almost
identical company — and later in this chapter we will watch it fail, with
real numbers.

But it has one property that made the entire field possible: it needs no
labels. Raw text is the supervision. That property made it possible to learn
representations from large unlabelled collections, and it made data scale a
central advantage in NLP.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What does "similar" mean here?** Distributional similarity is not the same as
synonymy. `cat` and `dog` are the same kind of thing; `doctor` and `hospital`
are related; `hot` and `cold` are opposites that keep the same company. That
distinction comes back later in this chapter, when we read cosine similarity.
:::

## Count first: co-occurrence, PPMI, SVD

Before word2vec there was a recipe, and it had three steps: count what
appears near what, reweight the counts so common words stop dominating, then
factorize.

We are going to do all three by hand. Partly because it makes everything
later much less mysterious, and partly because @levy2014neural showed that
word2vec is quietly doing the same thing anyway.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**The three steps in this section.**

1. **Count.** Which words appear in which contexts?
2. **Reweight.** Pull down counts that look high only because a word is
   frequent.
3. **Compress.** Represent the repeated patterns in fewer dimensions.
:::

Here is a corpus of ten sentences, small enough to check every number.

```python
import numpy as np

corpus = [
    "the king rules the castle",
    "the queen rules the castle",
    "the king eats an apple",
    "the queen eats a banana",
    "the royal castle is grand",
    "a banana is sweet fruit",
    "an apple is sweet fruit",
    "the man eats an apple",
    "the woman eats a banana",
    "the king and queen are royal",
]

tokens = [s.split() for s in corpus]
vocab = sorted({w for s in tokens for w in s})
idx = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}
V = len(vocab)
print("sentences:", len(corpus), " vocabulary:", V)
print(vocab)
```

```text
sentences: 10  vocabulary: 19
['a', 'an', 'and', 'apple', 'are', 'banana', 'castle', 'eats', 'fruit', 'grand', 'is', 'king', 'man', 'queen', 'royal', 'rules', 'sweet', 'the', 'woman']
```

### Step 1 — count what appears near what

The context of a word is a window around it. Window 2 means: two tokens to
the left, two to the right. Slide it over every position and add one to the
cell for every (word, neighbour) pair you see.

```python
W = 2
C = np.zeros((V, V))
for sent in tokens:
    for i, w in enumerate(sent):
        for j in range(max(0, i - W), min(len(sent), i + W + 1)):
            if i != j:
                C[idx[w], idx[sent[j]]] += 1
```

```text
### raw co-occurrence, a few rows
            eats   rules   royal   sweet     the  castle
king           1       1       0       0       4       0
queen          1       1       1       0       3       0
apple          2       0       0       1       0       0
banana         2       0       0       1       0       0
```

Already the structure is visible: `king` and `queen` have nearly the same
row, and so do `apple` and `banana`. That is the distributional hypothesis
working. The rows of $C$ *are* word vectors — 19-dimensional ones — and
unlike one-hots they are not orthogonal.

But they have chapter 2's disease.

```text
### the same problem as chapter 2: 'the' dominates
  the      total co-occurrences    22
  eats     total co-occurrences    16
  is       total co-occurrences    11
  queen    total co-occurrences    10
  king     total co-occurrences     9
  a        total co-occurrences     8
```

The largest number in the `king` row is `the`, which tells you nothing about
kings. Raw counts measure opportunity, not association.

### Step 2 — PPMI: from raw counts to unexpected co-occurrence

::: {#gloss-pointwise-mutual-information-pmi .column-margin .term-gloss}
**pointwise mutual information (PMI)** — how much more often two words
turn up together than they would if they were unrelated. It measures
surprise, not popularity. [↩](#term-pointwise-mutual-information-pmi){.term-back}
:::

We want to ask: *do these two words co-occur more often than chance would
predict?* [Pointwise mutual information](#gloss-pointwise-mutual-information-pmi){#term-pointwise-mutual-information-pmi .term-ref} asks exactly that.

$$
\mathrm{PMI}(w, c) = \log \frac{P(w, c)}{P(w)\,P(c)}
$$

Read the fraction like this: the denominator ($P(w)\,P(c)$) is how often we
would *expect* the two words to land next to each other if they were placed
completely independently; the numerator ($P(w, c)$) is how often they
actually do. So PMI is nothing but the log of **observed ÷ expected**. Three
cases:

- **Ratio 1** — the words co-occur exactly as often as chance predicts, so
  there is no relationship at all. $\log 1 = 0$, and PMI is zero.
- **Ratio above 1** — they co-occur more often than expected; they *attract*.
  The log is positive.
- **Ratio below 1** — they co-occur less often than expected; they *avoid*
  each other. The log is negative.

The negative side is notoriously unreliable, because establishing that two
words co-occur *less*
than chance takes far more data than establishing that they co-occur more.
So we clip at zero and call it [positive PMI]{.hl}.

$$
\mathrm{PPMI}(w, c) = \max\!\left(0,\ \log \frac{c_{wc}\, N}{c_{w\ast}\, c_{\ast c}}\right)
$$

Here $c_{wc}$ is how often the pair actually occurred, $c_{w\ast}$ is the row
total, $c_{\ast c}$ the column total, and $N$ the grand total of the matrix.
That fraction is doing something very simple, and it is worth seeing it with
actual numbers.

**Work one cell by hand.** We will run the formula on `apple`–`sweet`, but
first pin down where the four numbers come from, because all four are read
off the same matrix $C$:

- $c_{wc} = 1$ — how many times `apple` and `sweet` actually landed in each
  other's window. That is a single cell, visible in the table above.
- $c_{w\ast} = 7$ — the **sum of the `apple` row**, meaning "how many times
  was `apple` counted next to anything at all". `apple` occurs three times in
  the corpus, with 2, 3 and 2 neighbours respectively: $2 + 3 + 2 = 7$.
- $c_{\ast c} = 6$ — the same sum for `sweet`, down its **column**.
- $N = 144$ — the sum of every cell in the matrix: all the (word, neighbour)
  pairs counted in the corpus. You can check it by hand. Each token
  contributes one pair per neighbour in its window — 4 for a token in the
  middle of a sentence, 2 or 3 at the edges — so a five-token sentence yields
  14 pairs. The corpus has nine five-token sentences and one six-token
  sentence (18 pairs): $9 \times 14 + 18 = 144$.

Note that $N$ is not the 51 tokens in the corpus; it is the number of
*pairs*. Because the denominator of PMI is a product of probabilities, the
thing to divide by is how many pairs were counted, not how many tokens exist.

Now the actual question: if the two words were sprinkled through the text
completely independently, how many times would we *expect* them to land next
to each other?

$$
\frac{c_{\text{apple},\ast} \times c_{\ast,\text{sweet}}}{N}
= \frac{7 \times 6}{144} = 0.29
$$

We observed 1, which is $1 / 0.29 = 3.43$ times more than expected. PMI is
the log of that ratio: $\log 3.43 = 1.23$ — the value in the table.

Now do the same for `king`–`the`, which occurs **four** times — exactly four
times as often as `apple`–`sweet`. But `the` is everywhere: its column sums
to 22, and the `king` row sums to 9. By chance alone we already expect
$9 \times 22 / 144 = 1.38$ co-occurrences, so this pair had every reason to
meet.

Put the two calculations side by side:

| | observed | expected | ratio | PMI |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| `apple`–`sweet` | 1 | $7 \times 6 / 144 = 0.29$ | 3.43 | **1.23** |
| `king`–`the` | 4 | $9 \times 22 / 144 = 1.38$ | 2.91 | **1.07** |

: The raw count loses, the ratio wins {tbl-colwidths="[24,17,29,15,15]"}

The pair seen once scores **higher** than the pair seen four times. The
reason is right there: most of the four meetings between `king` and `the` are
explained by how popular `the` is, whereas the single meeting between `apple`
and `sweet` is not explained by anything. That reversal is the entire point
of the formula.

::: {.column-margin}
Think of a crowded party. Someone who talks to everyone tells you nothing
when you see them with the guest of honour — you expected that. Someone who
talks to only three people all evening, and one of them is the guest of
honour, tells you a great deal. PMI is the arithmetic of that intuition:
divide what you saw by what you had every reason to expect.
:::

```python
total = C.sum()
row = C.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
col = C.sum(axis=0, keepdims=True)
with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
    pmi = np.log((C * total) / (row * col))
pmi[~np.isfinite(pmi)] = 0.0
PPMI = np.maximum(pmi, 0.0)
```

```text
### PPMI for the same cells
            eats   rules   royal   sweet     the  castle
king        0.00    0.69    0.00    0.00    1.07    0.00
queen       0.00    0.59    1.06    0.00    0.67    0.00
apple       0.94    0.00    0.00    1.23    0.00    0.00
banana      0.94    0.00    0.00    1.23    0.00    0.00
```

Compare with the raw table. `apple`–`sweet` was a count of 1, the smallest
non-zero number in the row; it is now 1.23, the *largest* value in the row.
The count was small because `sweet` is rare, and PPMI divides that out.

::: {.column-margin}
PPMI and IDF are not the same formula, but they share an engineering
instinct: a high raw count is not information on its own. IDF measures how
rare a term is across the documents of a collection, and contributes to its
weight in a particular document once combined with TF. PMI checks whether two
words meet often only because each of them is frequent.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Intuition check: why clip the negatives instead of keeping them?

Suppose two words each occur 10 times in a million-token corpus and never
co-occur. Expected co-occurrence under independence is about 0.0002, so
observing zero is completely unsurprising — it carries no evidence that
the two words avoid each other. But $\log(0)$ is $-\infty$, and even
smoothed it produces a large negative number that dominates the vector.

Negative PMI values are dominated by sampling noise for exactly the words
you have least data about, which is most of them. Clipping is a crude but
effective admission that we cannot estimate them. It also has a pleasant
side effect: it keeps the matrix sparse, and @levy2015improving found that
tuned PPMI is competitive with word2vec on most benchmarks — the gap people
attributed to neural networks was largely a gap in hyperparameter care.
:::

### Step 3 — collect the repeated structure in a few dimensions

The PPMI rows already behave sensibly:

```text
### nearest neighbours before factorization (PPMI rows, 19-D)
  king     queen 0.55, are 0.55, man 0.45, the 0.37
  apple    man 0.79, fruit 0.52, banana 0.40, is 0.31
  eats     a 0.55, an 0.55, man 0.34, woman 0.34
```

`king` → `queen` is right. `apple` → `man` is not, and it is worth looking at:
both appear in *the man eats an apple*, so a single shared sentence in a
ten-sentence corpus is enough to fake an association. Sparse count vectors
are brittle exactly where data is thin.

::: {#gloss-singular-value-decomposition-svd .column-margin .term-gloss}
**singular value decomposition (SVD)** — a standard way of finding the few
directions in a large table that carry most of its variation, so you can
keep those and discard the rest. [↩](#term-singular-value-decomposition-svd){.term-back}
:::

In the toy corpus 19 dimensions cost nothing to compute; the point here is to
watch what a low-rank representation does to the $V$-dimensional vectors of a
real system.

Truncated [singular value decomposition](#gloss-singular-value-decomposition-svd){#term-singular-value-decomposition-svd .term-ref} gives you a regularisation
and compression mechanism against this. Keep only the $d$ directions with the
largest singular values and you force the model to spend its budget on the
structure that recurs, leaving one-off coincidences only whatever room is left
over. It is not a guarantee of correctness: on a small or biased corpus a
low-rank model can generalise the wrong structure too.

$$
\mathrm{PPMI} \approx U_d \Sigma_d V_d^\top, \qquad
\text{embedding} = U_d \Sigma_d
$$

We use the rows of $U_d \Sigma_d$ as each word's coordinates in this chapter.
The literature also uses $U_d$, or variants that scale the singular values by
other powers; the measured consequences of that choice come up just below.

Is that notation unfamiliar? Then here is the picture behind it.

Think of the PPMI matrix as a stack of transparencies. Each one shows a single
recurring pattern — *these words tend to sit near those words* — and each is
printed at a different darkness. Stack all 19 and you reproduce the original
matrix exactly.

The singular values in $\Sigma$ are those darknesses, sorted from boldest to
faintest. $U$ says how much each word participates in each pattern.

Truncating to $d$ means keeping only the boldest few transparencies. The
faint ones are where a coincidence lives: a pattern that a single sentence
created and nothing else confirms. Dropping them is not a regrettable loss of
information, it is the *mechanism*. Forcing 19 columns of evidence through 5
numbers means the model can only afford to store what repeats.

::: {.column-margin}
This is the same bargain as a low bit-rate audio file. You are not asking for
a worse recording; you are asking the encoder to spend its budget on what
matters and let the rest go. When the budget is tight enough, hiss is the
first thing to disappear.
:::

```python
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(PPMI, full_matrices=False)
emb = U[:, :d] * S[:d]
```

Multiplying by `S` weights each direction by how much of the matrix it
explains, and that is the textbook choice. It is also, on the evidence, the
wrong default. @levy2015improving swept the whole family
$W = U_d \Sigma_d^{\,p}$ and found $p = 0.5$ — often even $p = 0$, dropping
$\Sigma$ entirely — beating $p = 1$ by up to fifteen points on similarity
benchmarks. The mechanism is one this chapter meets again later: $\Sigma$ loads
the dominant direction most heavily, and the dominant direction is largely
frequency, which is precisely the anisotropy we will measure as a *defect*
sixty lines from now. We keep $p = 1$ here because it keeps the arithmetic
visible; in production, sweep $p$.

```text
### singular values (how much structure each dimension carries)
  5.75  4.76  4.03  3.71  3.64  3.08  3.03  2.80
  first 2 dimensions hold 36.8% of the sum of squares
  first 5 dimensions hold 65.4% of the sum of squares

### nearest neighbours after SVD to 5 dimensions
  king     queen 0.90, are 0.88, the 0.74, castle 0.65
  apple    banana 1.00, woman 0.86, man 0.85, fruit 0.74
  eats     an 0.95, a 0.95, man 0.64, woman 0.63
  castle   are 0.82, is 0.80, king 0.65, queen 0.61
```

Those percentages are shares of the *squared* singular values, which is the
conventional way to report how much of a matrix a set of directions accounts
for. Five directions out of nineteen carry roughly two-thirds of it — the
remaining fourteen are splitting the last third between them, which is
another way of saying none of them is describing much.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Deep dive: what SVD "explains" is not PCA's variance

Strictly the share is of the total sum of squares $\lVert X \rVert_F^2$ and not
of variance — the PPMI matrix is never centred, so these shares are not
variance shares. (Uncentred data has a variance too; it is simply not what this
quantity measures.) The two coincide only after centring, which is what makes
the thirty-word PCA plot later in this chapter a genuinely different
calculation.
:::

The easiest way to see what happened is to put three cosines side by side,
before and after factorization:

| word pair | PPMI rows, 19-D | SVD, 5-D | what happened |
|---|--:|--:|---|
| `apple` – `banana` | 0.40 | **1.00** | never share a sentence in this corpus; the shared contexts already link them, and the compression is what makes the link decisive |
| `king` – `queen` | 0.55 | **0.90** | already right, and got stronger |
| `apple` – `man` | 0.79 | **0.85** | the one-sentence accident — *not* deleted, but no longer first |

: The same counts, compressed into five dimensions {tbl-colwidths="[24,20,16,40]"}

Look at the third row, because this step is usually described wrongly.

SVD does **not** delete the `apple`–`man` accident. That cosine *rises*, from
0.79 to 0.85. What changes is the ranking: before, `apple`'s nearest neighbour
was `man` with `banana` third; now `banana` is first and `man` third.

So the compression does not break the wrong link. It strengthens the right one
enough to overtake it — and that is what "preferring signal over noise"
actually looks like. The ordering improves; the absolute values do not.

The number to watch is the first row. `apple` and `banana` never once occur
in the same sentence in this corpus, so nothing links them *directly*. What
links them is that they keep the same company — both follow `eats`, both
precede `is sweet fruit`. The raw PPMI rows already register that as a cosine
of 0.40, because shared contexts are shared coordinates; what the compression
does is strengthen it to 1.00, enough to reorder the neighbour list. Call this
shared-context generalisation rather than transitivity — cosine similarity is
not a transitive relation in the mathematical sense — and note that low-rank
compression is what makes it decisive rather than what makes it visible.

This is latent semantic analysis [@deerwester1990indexing], and it came before
word2vec by more than twenty years.

```text
### compression
  one-hot / count row : 19 numbers per word
  svd embedding       : 5 numbers per word
  any two one-hots    : cosine 0.00 (always)
  king vs queen (2-D) : cosine 0.996
  king vs banana(2-D) : cosine 0.141
```

Read 0.996 with the caveat in the box below already in mind: in a
two-dimensional space where every word shares the sign of the first
coordinate, a high cosine is partly the shared direction talking, not the
similarity.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**A detail worth noticing, because it comes back at the end of the chapter.**
In this toy space every single word has a *negative* first coordinate. A
dimension that all words share the sign of cannot separate any of them — it
is a common direction, not a contrastive one. Plotting dimensions 1 and 2
therefore wastes half the picture, which is why the figure below plots
dimensions 2 and 3.

Real embedding spaces have the same defect at scale, where it is called
[anisotropy]{.hl}, and we will measure it on GloVe later.
:::

## From counting to predicting: word2vec

So counting works. We built a space by hand, and royalty landed on one side
and food on the other. Why were prediction-based methods like word2vec taken up
so quickly?

Scalability was one of the main reasons. The co-occurrence matrix is
vocabulary-by-vocabulary. At 100,000 words that is ten billion *possible*
cells — sparse storage keeps only the non-zeros, but it is still one monolithic
artifact you have to build before you can factorize anything. word2vec proposed
a different route: rather than build that matrix explicitly, learn the same
distributional signal from local prediction tasks. The field did not abandon
counting — GloVe, a few pages from here, and the comparison table at the end of
this chapter are both evidence of that.

::: {#gloss-word2vec .column-margin .term-gloss}
**word2vec** — the 2013 method that learns embeddings by training a model
to guess nearby words, then keeping the numbers it learned along the way
and throwing the model itself out. [↩](#term-word2vec){.term-back}
:::

In 2013 Mikolov and colleagues published [word2vec](#gloss-word2vec){#term-word2vec .term-ref}, a method that skipped the
matrix entirely [@mikolov2013efficient; @mikolov2013distributed]. Rather than
counting co-occurrences and factorizing, train a classifier to *predict*
context — and then throw the classifier away and keep its weights.

Architecturally, that classifier is a **shallow neural network**: an input
layer, a single hidden layer, an output layer. It is called shallow because
there is only one hidden layer and — unlike a deep network — it carries no
activation function. The three layers do this:

1. The **input layer** is a word's one-hot vector: as long as the vocabulary,
   a single 1, zeros everywhere else.
2. The **hidden layer** multiplies that vector by a matrix $\mathbf{W}$.
   Multiplying a one-hot by a matrix does nothing except pull out the row
   belonging to that word — so the hidden layer is really a lookup table. The
   row it pulls out *is* the word's embedding. No sums, no activation, which
   is why it is often called a *projection layer* instead.
3. The **output layer** is a second matrix, $\mathbf{W}'$. It scores the
   hidden vector against candidate words from the vocabulary.

The critical point: [the product is not the network you train, it is the
weights of the network's first layer.]{.hl} When training ends, $\mathbf{W}'$
is thrown away and $\mathbf{W}$ is what you keep — one row per word, 300
numbers per row. The model was a pretext; the weights were the point. You
will see why that matters in @sec-transformers: the embedding table at the
bottom of a transformer is the same kind of object: a learned table with one row per word.

There are two ways to set up that prediction, and they are mirror images. Same
window, same words, arrows reversed:

| Architecture | Input | Predicts |
|---|---|---|
| **Skip-gram** | the centre word | the context words |
| **CBOW** | the context words | the centre word |

: The two word2vec architectures {tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

This chapter follows skip-gram, which is also what negative sampling is most
often paired with.

and both throw **W′** away at the end. The vectors you download are the rows
of **W**.

::::

Skip-gram is the variant that won, and the rest of this chapter uses it.
Slide a window over the corpus and every position yields training examples.

::: {.anlp-widget}
```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">Skip-gram — type a sentence and watch the training pairs appear</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof sgSentence = Inputs.text({
  label: "Sentence",
  value: "the pump failed during the night shift",
  width: 420
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof sgWindow = Inputs.range([1, 4], {label: "Window size", step: 1, value: 2})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
sgTokens = (sgSentence || "").toLowerCase().split(/\s+/).filter(t => t.length)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof sgCentre = Inputs.range([0, Math.max(0, sgTokens.length - 1)],
  {label: "Centre position", step: 1, value: 1})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
sgPairs = {
  const out = [];
  sgTokens.forEach((w, i) => {
    for (let j = Math.max(0, i - sgWindow);
         j <= Math.min(sgTokens.length - 1, i + sgWindow); j++) {
      if (i !== j) out.push({centre: w, context: sgTokens[j], ci: i, cj: j});
    }
  });
  return out;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div style="font-size:0.9rem;">
  <div style="margin:0.5rem 0 0.7rem 0;">
    ${sgTokens.map((t, i) => {
      const c = i === sgCentre;
      const inWin = Math.abs(i - sgCentre) <= sgWindow && i !== sgCentre;
      return html`<code style="background:${c ? "#0E7C7B" : inWin ? "#D6EAE9" : "#F4F6F8"};
        color:${c ? "#fff" : "#1E2229"};
        border:1px solid ${c ? "#0E7C7B" : "currentColor"}; border-radius:0.35em;
        padding:0.12em 0.42em; margin-right:0.25em;">${t}</code>`;
    })}
  </div>
  <p style="color:var(--fig-muted); margin:0 0 0.5rem 0;">
    Centre <b>${sgTokens[sgCentre] ?? "—"}</b> produces
    <b>${sgPairs.filter(p => p.ci === sgCentre).length}</b> pairs.
    The whole sentence produces <b>${sgPairs.length}</b>.
  </p>
  <div>
    ${sgPairs.filter(p => p.ci === sgCentre).map(p => html`<span
      style="display:inline-block; border:1px solid var(--fig-border); border-radius:0.4em;
      padding:0.15em 0.5em; margin:0 0.3em 0.3em 0; font-size:0.85rem;">
      (<b>${p.centre}</b>, ${p.context})</span>`)}
  </div>
  <p style="color:var(--fig-muted); margin-top:0.7rem; font-size:0.85rem;">
    This is the entire supervision signal. No labels, no annotation — just
    the text, cut into pairs. A corpus of 6 billion tokens with window 5
    yields about 60 billion of these.</p>
</div>`
```
:::

### Negative sampling is a logistic regression

There is one problem left, and it is a bad one. To turn a score into a
probability you normalise over the whole vocabulary — which means every
single training pair costs you a sum over 400,000 words. Sixty billion pairs,
each costing 400,000 operations, is not a training run anybody finishes.

The fix is almost embarrassingly simple, and it is the reason word2vec was
practical.

::: {#gloss-negative-sampling .column-margin .term-gloss}
**negative sampling** — instead of scoring every word in the vocabulary,
score the true neighbour against a handful of randomly drawn fake ones.
A cheap yes/no question replaces an impossibly expensive one. [↩](#term-negative-sampling){.term-back}
:::

Predicting a context word out of a 400,000-word vocabulary means a softmax
over 400,000 classes, for every one of billions of pairs. That is
hopeless. The trick that made word2vec practical replaces it with a question
a statistician will recognise instantly [@mikolov2013distributed]:

> Given a pair of words, is this a *real* pair from the corpus, or one I made
> up?

That is binary classification. For each real pair $(w, c)$, draw $K$ fake
context words from a noise distribution and label them 0 — that drawing is
the [negative sampling](#gloss-negative-sampling){#term-negative-sampling .term-ref} the method is named after. Then fit a
logistic regression whose linear predictor is the dot product of the two
words' vectors:

$$
P(\text{real} \mid w, c) = \sigma(\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c),
\qquad \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}
$$

Unlike ordinary logistic regression the features are not fixed: the centre and
context vectors are learned at the same time, which makes the problem
non-convex once the two tables are considered together.

The rest is minimising the usual log loss:

$$
\mathcal{L} = -\log \sigma(\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c)
- \sum_{k=1}^{K} \log \sigma(-\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_{n_k})
$$

Read it in two halves. The first term is small when $\sigma(\mathbf{v}_w \cdot
\mathbf{u}_c)$ is close to 1, so it pays you for giving *real* pairs a large
dot product. The second term is small when $\sigma(-\mathbf{v}_w \cdot
\mathbf{u}_{n_k})$ is close to 1 — that is, when the dot product with each
*fake* partner is very negative. One term pulls together, $K$ terms push
apart. Those two terms are the whole objective.

**Work one update by hand.** Vectors are 300-dimensional in practice; use 4
so the arithmetic fits on a line. Say the centre word `failed` currently has
$\mathbf{v} = (0.4,\ -0.2,\ 0.7,\ 0.1)$, its true partner `pump` has
$\mathbf{u} = (0.5,\ 0.1,\ 0.6,\ -0.3)$, and a sampled fake `opera` has
$\mathbf{u} = (-0.3,\ 0.6,\ -0.2,\ 0.4)$.

For the real pair, the dot product is

$$
(0.4)(0.5) + (-0.2)(0.1) + (0.7)(0.6) + (0.1)(-0.3) = 0.57
$$

so $\sigma(0.57) = 0.639$ — the model currently gives this pair a 64% chance
of being genuine — and its contribution to the loss is $-\log 0.639 = 0.448$.

For the fake pair the dot product is $-0.34$, giving $\sigma(0.34) = 0.584$
and a loss of $-\log 0.584 = 0.538$. The model is already leaning the right
way on both, but not confidently, so both will be nudged.

The nudge itself is where the whole thing becomes recognisable. The
derivative of the loss with respect to the dot product is just

$$
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial (\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c)}
= \sigma(\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c) - y
$$

where $y$ is 1 for a real pair and 0 for a fake one. **Prediction minus
target** — the same expression that falls out of every logistic regression
you have ever fitted. For `pump` that is $0.639 - 1 = -0.361$ (negative, so
the dot product goes up); for `opera` it is $0.416 - 0 = 0.416$ (positive, so
the dot product goes down).

Both vectors in a pair move. The collapsed derivation below shows the two
gradients, and each vector is dragged along the direction of the other.

To keep the arithmetic followable, let us hold the context vectors
$\mathbf{u}$ fixed and update only the centre vector $\mathbf{v}$. Its
gradient is the *sum* of both terms — that is what the loss above says, and
what `gv` in the training code below computes in one `einsum`:

$$
g_{\mathbf v} = (0.639 - 1)\,\mathbf u_{\texttt{pump}}
              + (0.416 - 0)\,\mathbf u_{\texttt{opera}}
              = (-0.305,\ 0.213,\ -0.300,\ 0.275)
$$

With a learning rate of 0.05 that moves `failed`·`pump` from 0.570 to **0.590**
and `failed`·`opera` from $-0.340$ to $-0.359$.

Update the context vectors too, as a real implementation does, and the same
step lands on **0.603** and $-0.374$ — the same directions, moved about 1.6
times as far.

Those are tiny movements. Multiply them by tens of billions of pairs and you
get the geometry that made these models famous, which is the honest summary
of how word2vec works: no cleverness, just an enormous number of very small
corrections.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The gradient in full, for the reader who wants to see it fall out

Take the real-pair term alone, and write $z = \mathbf{v}_w \cdot
\mathbf{u}_c$. The single fact you need is that the sigmoid has an
unusually tidy derivative:

$$
\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)\,\bigl(1 - \sigma(z)\bigr)
$$

Now differentiate $-\log \sigma(z)$ with the chain rule:

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\bigl[-\log \sigma(z)\bigr]
= -\frac{\sigma'(z)}{\sigma(z)}
= -\frac{\sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z))}{\sigma(z)}
= \sigma(z) - 1
$$

The $\sigma(z)$ cancels, which is the whole reason log loss is paired with
the sigmoid rather than, say, squared error. For a negative sample the term
is $-\log \sigma(-z)$ and the same two lines give $\sigma(z)$. Both cases
collapse into $\sigma(z) - y$.

Getting from there to the vectors is one more chain-rule step, because
$\partial z / \partial \mathbf{v}_w = \mathbf{u}_c$:

$$
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{v}_w}
= \bigl(\sigma(z) - y\bigr)\, \mathbf{u}_c,
\qquad
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{u}_c}
= \bigl(\sigma(z) - y\bigr)\, \mathbf{v}_w
$$

Each vector is dragged along the direction of the other, by an amount equal
to how wrong the prediction was. A pair the model already scores correctly
produces a near-zero gradient and is effectively skipped; the learning
concentrates on pairs it is currently getting wrong. That self-limiting
behaviour is why the method survives billions of updates without
diverging — and why the implementation later in this chapter needs gradient
clipping only when many updates for the same word are batched together.
:::

```{=html}
  <text x="628" y="206" class="t-xs t-muted">fake</text>
  <text x="628" y="235" class="t-xs t-muted">fake</text>

  <text x="402" y="266" class="t-sm"><tspan class="t-b">6</tspan> dot products, no</text>
  <text x="402" y="282" class="t-sm">normalization — <tspan class="t-b">per pair</tspan>.</text>
</svg>
```

::: {.fig-cap}
The left panel asks *which of 400,000 words comes next* — one question with
400,000 answers. The right panel asks *is this pair real?* six times — six
questions with two answers each. The second is a logistic regression, and it
is roughly 67,000 times cheaper.
:::
::::

Notice how the two descriptions meet here.

The network *does* have a hidden layer — the row pulled out of $\mathbf{W}$ is
exactly that. But it carries no activation function, and the only
non-linearity in the whole model is the sigmoid at the very end. A single
linear layer with no activation, followed by a sigmoid and a log loss, is by
definition a logistic regression.

So "shallow neural network" and "logistic regression" are not competing
explanations. They are two names for the same object: reach for the first to
describe the architecture, the second to compute the gradient.

If you have ever fitted a logistic regression, you have fitted 99% of
word2vec. The
only unusual part is that *both* the predictors and the coefficients are
learned, which is what makes it a factorization rather than a regression.

::: {.column-margin}
Two matrices are learned, not one: $\mathbf{v}_w$ for words as centres and
$\mathbf{u}_c$ for words as contexts. Almost everyone discards $\mathbf{u}$
and keeps $\mathbf{v}$. Adding them sometimes helps a little; GloVe's
authors recommend it [@pennington2014glove].
:::

:::

### Which vectors get updated in one step?

This is the question to settle before writing the code, and the answer on its
own explains why word2vec is fast.

For a single training pair, with $K = 5$ negatives, there are **seven row
updates** across the two matrices:

- **one** row of $\mathbf{W}$: the centre word's vector $\mathbf{v}_w$.
- **one** row of $\mathbf{W}'$: the true context word's vector
  $\mathbf{u}_c$.
- **$K$** rows of $\mathbf{W}'$: the vectors of the sampled fake words.

If the sampled negatives repeat, or collide with the true context word, the
number of *distinct* rows touched is fewer than seven; the number of update
contributions does not change.

Everything else — the rows of every other word in the vocabulary, in both
matrices — **does not move**. Not "moves a little": the gradients are
*exactly zero*. The reason is simple. Those rows never entered any dot
product in this step, so they never appear in the loss, and the derivative
with respect to a parameter that does not appear in the loss is zero.

For scale, take the model we train from scratch below: a vocabulary of
18,677, 100
dimensions, two matrices — 37,354 rows and 3,735,400 parameters. One training
pair touches **7 rows**, which is **0.019%** of them. That is why billions of
updates finish in hours on one machine.

You can see it directly in the update lines of the code below: `targets` in
`np.add.at(Wo, targets.ravel(), ...)` holds only $K+1$ indices per pair, so
only that many rows of `Wo` are added into. The rest are untouched.

**With a full softmax it would be completely different**, and the difference
is precisely why negative sampling exists. The softmax denominator sums over
*every* word in the vocabulary, so every word's output vector enters the loss
and every one of them receives a non-zero gradient. Rows touched per pair
jumps from 7 to 18,678 — half of all rows — which is **2,668 times** the
arithmetic, for *every* pair.

::: {.column-margin}
The practical consequence: the gradient of an embedding matrix is **sparse**.
PyTorch's `nn.Embedding(..., sparse=True)` and the matching `SparseAdam`
optimizer come straight out of this fact. A second consequence: a word learns
only as much as it occurs in the corpus or gets drawn as a negative. That is
another way to read why the 0.75 exponent matters — it buys tail words a
place in the update queue.
:::

### Two training details that decide how well word2vec works

**Subsampling frequent words.** Very frequent words produce most of the
training pairs while carrying little discriminative information: *the* appears
next to everything. So rather than keep every occurrence, we discard tokens
with a probability that depends on frequency. word2vec keeps word $w$ with
probability

$$
p_{\text{keep}}(w) = \min\!\left(1,\ \left(\sqrt{\frac{f(w)}{t}} + 1\right)\cdot\frac{t}{f(w)}\right),
\qquad t \approx 10^{-3}
$$

The formula looks arbitrary until you put numbers through it. The threshold
$t = 10^{-3}$ is the pivot: any word making up less than a thousandth of the
corpus comes out with the inner expression above 1 and is simply always kept,
which is what the $\min$ is doing.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Deep dive: the formula in the paper and the formula in the code

The form above is the one in word2vec's original C source, and a good share of
common implementations follow that behaviour; the published paper states a
different one, $P(\text{discard}) = 1 - \sqrt{t/f}$. The two disagree, and the
code is what was actually run — a small but useful reminder to read the
implementation, not only the paper.
:::

| share of corpus | example | $p_{\text{keep}}$ | discarded |
|---|---|--:|--:|
| 5% | `the` in English text | 0.16 | 84% |
| 1% | `of`, `and` | 0.42 | 58% |
| 0.1% ($=t$) | mid-frequency word | 1.00 | 0% |
| 0.01% and below | everything in the tail | 1.00 | 0% |

: What subsampling actually throws away {tbl-colwidths="[22,30,24,24]"}

So this is not a gentle reweighting. It deletes five out of every six
occurrences of `the`, and it does not touch the tail at all — rare words are
left alone while the top of the Zipf curve you plotted in @sec-text-as-data
is aggressively thinned.

In the run below it discards 26.6% of the in-vocabulary tokens: 6,397,826
become 4,698,743. Almost all of what it throws away is `the`, `of`, `and` and
their friends.

(Where does 6,397,826 come from? It is what is left of the run's
`tokens read: 6794527` once everything below `min_count=20` is dropped. The
subsampling rate applies to that.)

::: {.column-margin}
There is a second, less obvious benefit. Deleting a token also *widens* the
windows around it: with `the` removed, the words either side of it become
neighbours. Subsampling does not only remove uninformative pairs, it creates
informative ones.
:::

**The 0.75 exponent.** Negative samples are not drawn from the unigram
distribution but from $P(w) \propto f(w)^{0.75}$. Raising every probability to
a power below 1 pulls all of them toward 1, and it pulls the smallest ones
furthest in relative terms: $0.5^{0.75}$ is 19% larger than $0.5$, while
$0.001^{0.75}$ is 5.6 times larger than $0.001$. Renormalising afterwards
therefore moves probability mass out of the head of the distribution and into
the tail.

Concretely: if a common word is 5,000 times more frequent than a rare one,
then after the exponent it is only $5000^{0.75} \approx 595$ times more
likely to be drawn as a negative. The gap narrows by a factor of about eight,
and it narrows in the rare word's favour.

Why does that matter? Because being sampled as a negative teaches a word not
only which contexts to move towards but which contexts to move away from. A
word never drawn as a negative is never explicitly pushed away from anything,
and its vector simply drifts.

So the exponent buys the tail of the vocabulary a share of the training signal
its raw frequency would never earn it.

And it was chosen empirically — 0.75 has no derivation behind it. It is also
one of the hyperparameters @levy2015improving identified as doing much of the
work people were crediting to the model.

### Deep dive: writing word2vec from scratch

For the main storyline, the training loop is six steps:

1. take a real (centre, context) pair from the corpus;
2. draw $K$ fake context words from the noise distribution;
3. compute the dot products between the centre vector and those $K+1$ vectors;
4. apply the sigmoid;
5. take the error, prediction minus label;
6. update the corresponding rows of the two tables with that error.

What follows is that loop, running. If the numerical details — batching,
sampling, gradient clipping — are not what you are here for, skip to the
results.

Roughly sixty lines of NumPy, trained on the first 40 million characters of
`text8` (a cleaned dump of English Wikipedia). No deep learning framework —
the update rule below is the gradient of the log loss above, written out.

```python
import gzip, time
from collections import Counter
import numpy as np
import gensim.downloader as api

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

with gzip.open(api.load("text8", return_path=True), "rt") as f:
    raw = f.read(40_000_000).split()

MIN_COUNT = 20
counts = Counter(raw)
vocab = [w for w, c in counts.most_common() if c >= MIN_COUNT]
idx = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}
V = len(vocab)

total = sum(counts[w] for w in vocab)
freq = np.array([counts[w] / total for w in vocab])
keep = np.minimum(1.0, (np.sqrt(freq / 1e-3) + 1) * (1e-3 / freq))

ids = np.array([idx[w] for w in raw if w in idx], dtype=np.int32)
ids = ids[rng.random(len(ids)) < keep[ids]]          # subsampling

noise = freq ** 0.75                                  # the 0.75 exponent
noise /= noise.sum()
cum = np.cumsum(noise)

D, K, WINDOW, EPOCHS, LR0 = 100, 5, 5, 3, 0.02
Wc = ((rng.random((V, D)) - 0.5) / D).astype(np.float32)   # centre vectors
Wo = np.zeros((V, D), dtype=np.float32)                    # context vectors

# Two simplifications, stated so you can undo them. The window is fixed at 5,
# whereas word2vec samples an effective width uniformly from {1..5} for each
# centre, which weights near neighbours more heavily. And pairs are formed
# across the whole token stream, ignoring document boundaries — harmless on
# text8, which is one continuous dump, wrong on a corpus of separate documents.
centres, contexts = [], []
for off in range(1, WINDOW + 1):
    centres.append(ids[:-off]); contexts.append(ids[off:])
    centres.append(ids[off:]); contexts.append(ids[:-off])
centres = np.concatenate(centres)
contexts = np.concatenate(contexts)
N = len(centres)

BATCH = 2048
n_batches = N // BATCH

def sigmoid(x):
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-np.clip(x, -8, 8)))

for epoch in range(EPOCHS):
    for b in range(n_batches):
        # drawn WITH replacement: "3 epochs" means three times as many
        # pair-draws as there are pairs, not three passes. About 5% of pairs
        # are never drawn and some are drawn six times, so do not compare
        # EPOCHS=3 here with epochs=3 in gensim.
        sl = rng.integers(0, N, BATCH)
        c, o = centres[sl], contexts[sl]
        negs = np.searchsorted(cum, rng.random((BATCH, K))).astype(np.int32)
        targets = np.concatenate([o[:, None], negs], axis=1)   # (B, K+1)
        labels = np.zeros((BATCH, K + 1), dtype=np.float32)
        labels[:, 0] = 1.0                       # first column is the real pair

        v = Wc[c]                                              # (B, D)
        u = Wo[targets]                                        # (B, K+1, D)
        score = sigmoid(np.einsum("bkd,bd->bk", u, v))         # (B, K+1)
        err = (score - labels).astype(np.float32)              # the residual

        lr = LR0 * max(1e-4, 1 - (epoch * n_batches + b) / (EPOCHS * n_batches))
        gv = np.einsum("bk,bkd->bd", err, u)
        gu = err[:, :, None] * v[:, None, :]
        np.clip(gv, -1.0, 1.0, out=gv)
        np.clip(gu, -1.0, 1.0, out=gu)
        np.add.at(Wc, c, -lr * gv)
        np.add.at(Wo, targets.ravel(), (-lr * gu).reshape(-1, D))

E = Wc / (np.linalg.norm(Wc, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9)
```

Look at the line `err = score - labels`. That is *predicted minus observed* —
the residual of a logistic regression. Every gradient below it is that
residual times the other vector. If the statistics feels familiar, it should.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Intuition check: why does `np.add.at` need gradient clipping here?

Real word2vec updates one pair at a time, so a frequent word's vector is
refreshed between updates. Batching breaks that: `np.add.at` *accumulates*
every gradient for a repeated index and applies the sum in one step. In a
batch of 2048 pairs, a common word can appear a hundred times, so it
receives a hundred stacked updates computed from a vector that never moved.

Without clipping this run diverges to `nan` within half an epoch — which is
exactly what happened the first time it was run for this chapter, at learning
rate 0.05.

It is worth being precise about what the clip does, because it does not fix the
stacking described above. `np.clip` is applied to the *per-example* gradient,
before `np.add.at` sums the duplicates, so it bounds each contribution but not
the accumulated row update: a word appearing a hundred times in the batch can
still move by $100 \times \text{lr}$. What it actually prevents is a single
large residual multiplied by a context vector whose norm has grown. The clean
fix is to divide each row's accumulated gradient by how many times its index
occurred in the batch — `np.bincount(targets.ravel(), minlength=V)` gives the
counts. Be clear about what that buys: it bounds the step a frequent word takes
and stops the update scaling with batch frequency. It does not reproduce
sequential SGD, which recomputes the gradient at the parameters left by the
previous example; averaging gradients all evaluated at the same point is a
different update, with a different effective step size.
The clip is not a modelling choice; it is the cheap version, and the price of
vectorising an inherently sequential algorithm. It is also a good example of
why "I reimplemented the paper and it didn't work" is usually about
optimisation details rather than the equations.
:::

### The two families were one family all along

For a year the field treated counting (LSA, PPMI+SVD) and predicting
(word2vec) as rival philosophies — @baroni2014dont is the paper that framed it
as a contest and reported predicting winning. Then @levy2014neural proved that
skip-gram with negative sampling is *implicitly factorizing* a matrix — and
that matrix is PMI, shifted by $\log K$:

$$
\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c = \mathrm{PMI}(w, c) - \log K
$$

— at the optimum, with the dot products free to take any value. So
prediction-based SGNS and matrix-based methods are far closer than they looked:
the optimal dot products target a shifted PMI. The low-rank constraint,
different losses and sampling mean they still do not produce the same embedding
in practice.

Note that this is PMI, not the PPMI of route A, and the difference is not
cosmetic. The implicit matrix holds $-\infty$ in every cell for a pair that
never co-occurs, which no factorization can represent — which is exactly why
Levy and Goldberg go on to propose the *shifted positive* PMI matrix,
$\mathrm{SPPMI}(w,c) = \max(\mathrm{PMI}(w,c) - \log K,\ 0)$, as the explicit
matrix you would actually build. Note where the clipping lives: it is a patch
applied when you *construct* an explicit SPPMI matrix. Training SGNS clips
nothing — it simply never has to represent a $-\infty$, because it only ever
sees the pairs it samples.

Look closely at what that sentence claims. Nowhere in word2vec does anyone
build a PMI matrix — the algorithm only ever sees one pair at a time and
nudges two vectors. Yet if you let it run to convergence and then read off
the dot product for any pair of words, you get that pair's PMI, minus a
constant. The matrix was never constructed; it was *reached*.

The $-\log K$ term has a plain reading too. Raising $K$ means each real pair
is contrasted against more fakes, which lowers the target for every dot product
by the same fixed amount. Be careful with the intuition here: the shift is
uniform in the *implicit matrix*, and that is not the same as translating every
word vector by a common offset — no set of $d$-dimensional vectors reproduces a
constant added to every inner product exactly. In practice $K$ is still one of
the less important settings, which is an empirical observation rather than a
consequence of the algebra.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Deep dive: why SGNS learns a shifted PMI

Fix a single pair $(w, c)$ and ask what value of $z = \mathbf{v}_w \cdot
\mathbf{u}_c$ minimises the loss, treating $z$ as a free number rather than
something built from vectors. Over the whole corpus that pair contributes a
positive term proportional to its actual count, and a negative term
proportional to how often the sampler would produce it by accident, which is
$K$ times the chance of drawing $c$ at random. Writing those two weights as
$P(w,c)$ and $K \cdot P(w)P(c)$, the objective for that pair is

$$
P(w,c)\,\log \sigma(z) \;+\; K\,P(w)P(c)\,\log \sigma(-z)
$$

Differentiate with respect to $z$, using $\frac{d}{dz}\log\sigma(z) = 1 -
\sigma(z)$ and $\frac{d}{dz}\log\sigma(-z) = -\sigma(z)$, and set the result
to zero:

$$
P(w,c)\bigl(1 - \sigma(z)\bigr) = K\,P(w)P(c)\,\sigma(z)
$$

Solve for $\sigma(z)$, then convert back through $z = \log
\frac{\sigma(z)}{1-\sigma(z)}$:

$$
z = \log \frac{P(w,c)}{K\,P(w)P(c)}
  = \log \frac{P(w,c)}{P(w)P(c)} - \log K
  = \mathrm{PMI}(w,c) - \log K
$$

The one assumption doing real work is that $z$ can be chosen freely for every
pair. It cannot — the dot products all share the same underlying vectors, and
with $d$ far below the vocabulary size the model must compromise. What the
theorem fixes is the *target*; it says nothing about how the compromise is
made, and that is where the two routes part company. A truncated SVD minimises
squared reconstruction error and weights every cell of the matrix equally.
SGNS minimises a logistic loss weighted by how often each pair was actually
sampled. Both are low-rank approximations to the same target and they are
approximations under different losses, so at a given $d$ they do not
generally produce the same vectors.

A second assumption is hiding in the notation, and it matters because it
contradicts the code above. Writing the noise weight as
$K\,P(w)P(c)$ assumes negatives are drawn from the *raw* unigram distribution.
word2vec draws them from $P_\alpha(c) \propto f(c)^{0.75}$ instead — the
exponent from two sections ago — and carrying that through gives

$$
\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c
  = \log \frac{P(w,c)}{P(w)\,P_\alpha(c)} - \log K
$$

which is PMI computed against a *smoothed* context distribution.
@levy2015improving call this context distribution smoothing, and show it
transfers straight to PPMI+SVD, where it is worth several points. So the 0.75
exponent is not a sampling detail bolted onto the algorithm: it changes which
matrix the algorithm factorizes.
:::

```{=html}
    <line x1="590" y1="190" x2="590" y2="210"/>
  </g>

  <path d="M170,258 C170,290 220,292 236,294" class="ln" marker-end="url(#br-a)"/>
  <path d="M590,258 C590,290 540,292 524,294" class="ln" marker-end="url(#br-a)"/>

</svg>
```

::: {.fig-cap}
The routes look unrelated — one is linear algebra on a count matrix, the
other is stochastic gradient descent on a classifier — but @levy2014neural
showed they are aimed at the same target. Skip-gram with negative sampling is
implicitly factorizing the PMI matrix that route A approximates by clipping it
into PPMI, shifted by $\log K$. Aimed at, not landing on: the equivalence is
exact for unconstrained dot products, and at the low rank you actually use the
two optimise different losses.
:::
::::

@levy2015improving followed up by showing that once you give the
count-based methods the same hyperparameters word2vec quietly uses —
subsampling, context distribution smoothing, dynamic windows — the
performance gap mostly disappears.

The lesson generalises well beyond embeddings, and it is worth carrying into
every paper you read: when a new method beats an old one, some of the
improvement is the method and some is the tuning, and the split is rarely
reported.

Which leaves the practical question of when to take which route. Since they aim
at the same target and land close enough that @levy2015improving could not
separate them once the hyperparameters matched, the choice is mostly about
engineering:

| | [Counting]{.pro} (PPMI + SVD) | [Predicting]{.pro} (word2vec) |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | Holds a $V \times V$ matrix. Stored densely that is 160 billion cells at $V = 400{,}000$ — but nobody stores it densely: the matrix is sparse, and GloVe builds exactly this one, for exactly this vocabulary, to produce the vectors used throughout this chapter. The real cost is that it is a single monolithic artifact, expensive to build and expensive to update | Streams the corpus; memory is $V \times d$ regardless of corpus size |
| Corpus size | Comfortable on small corpora, where every count is precious | Needs a lot of text before the gradient noise averages out |
| Determinism | [Same input, same output — for an exact solver. Randomized truncated SVD, the default at scale, needs a fixed seed, and singular vectors are only determined up to a sign either way]{.pro} | [Random initialisation and sampling; two runs differ]{.con} |
| New data | [Recount and refactorize from scratch]{.con} | [Keep training from where you stopped]{.pro} |
| Inspectability | [Every intermediate is a table you can read]{.pro} | [Little to read mid-training beyond the loss and the current nearest neighbours]{.con} |
| Tuning burden | Window size, PPMI variant, $d$ | Window, $d$, $K$, subsampling $t$, learning rate, epochs |

: The same destination, different engineering {tbl-colwidths="[19,40,41]"}

One difference does not fit in that table because it is statistical rather
than practical, and for a reader with a statistics background it is the most
important one. Truncated SVD gives the best rank-$d$ approximation in Frobenius
norm — the Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem — which means it weights *every cell
equally*, and the overwhelming majority of cells in a PPMI matrix are zero. So
SVD spends most of its budget faithfully reproducing "these two words never
met", a fact it holds millions of copies of. SGNS never sees a cell it did not
sample, so it weights each cell by how often the pair actually occurred. That,
and not the neural framing, is where SGNS's advantage on rare words comes from
— and it is exactly the defect that GloVe's weighting function $f(X_{wc})$ was
designed to fix, as the next section shows. Read the three methods as three
answers to one question: *how much should a cell you barely observed count?*

The row that decides it in practice is new data. Counting is the better
pedagogy, the better choice for a modest corpus, and the only one of the two
that is deterministic and inspectable; predicting is what survives contact with
a corpus that keeps growing.

## GloVe: counting, with a loss function

If counting and predicting are the same thing underneath, an obvious question
follows: could you do the counting *explicitly* and still get the benefits of
gradient descent?

One sentence separates the three methods. PPMI+SVD transforms the whole
co-occurrence table first and factorizes it afterwards. word2vec does an
implicit factorization through local training pairs. GloVe keeps the global
counts explicitly and optimises low-dimensional vectors to account for those
counts directly.

GloVe [@pennington2014glove] took that synthesis seriously. Build the global
co-occurrence matrix, then fit vectors so that dot products reproduce log
co-occurrence counts, weighting rare pairs down:

$$
\mathcal{L} = \sum_{w,c} f(X_{wc})
\left(\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c + b_w + b_c - \log X_{wc}\right)^2
$$

This is weighted least squares on log counts, with a bias term per word —
about as classical as statistics gets. Take it apart piece by piece, because
every term is there for a reason.

**Why $\log X_{wc}$ and not $X_{wc}$?** Co-occurrence counts are Zipfian: a
few pairs occur millions of times, most occur once. Fitting raw counts would
mean the loss is entirely about `of the` and nothing else. Taking logs turns
those ratios into differences, which is the scale the structure actually
lives on.

**Why the bias terms?** This is the part worth pausing on. $b_w$ can absorb
anything that depends only on $w$, and $b_c$ anything that depends only on
$c$ — which is exactly the row and column totals. Fitting them means
$\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c$ is left to explain what is *left over* after
each word's overall frequency has been accounted for. Compare that to the
PMI formula at the start of this chapter: dividing by $c_{w\ast}$ and
$c_{\ast c}$ is subtracting their logs, and subtracting their logs is what
these biases learn to do. Once the biases absorb the overall frequency effects
of the word and the context, what remains is a PMI-like residual structure —
one GloVe fits rather than computes.

**Why $f(X_{wc})$?** Two problems need solving at once. A pair that never
co-occurs has $\log 0 = -\infty$, and a pair that co-occurs constantly would
swamp everything else. GloVe's weighting function handles both:

$$
f(x) = \begin{cases}
(x / x_{\max})^{3/4} & x < x_{\max} \\
1 & x \geq x_{\max}
\end{cases}
\qquad x_{\max} = 100
$$

| $X_{wc}$ | $f(X_{wc})$ | effect on that pair |
|--:|--:|---|
| 0 | 0.00 | never enters the objective — no $\log 0$ problem |
| 1 | 0.03 | counted, but barely |
| 10 | 0.18 | growing weight |
| 100 | 1.00 | full weight |
| 100,000 | 1.00 | *also* full weight — the cap has bitten |

: GloVe's weighting function, at $x_{\max} = 100$ {tbl-colwidths="[16,18,66]"}

Note what $f(0) = 0$ buys: the infinity never has to be evaluated, because
its coefficient is zero. And note the cap. A pair seen 100,000 times gets
exactly the same weight as one seen 100 times, so the most frequent pairs in
the corpus — which are also the least informative — cannot dominate the fit.
That is the same instinct as word2vec's subsampling, implemented as a weight
rather than as a deletion. The exponent is even the same 0.75.

The pretrained vectors are the ones most people reach for when they want
static embeddings, so we will use them for the rest of the chapter.

```python
import numpy as np
import gensim.downloader as api

g = api.load("glove-wiki-gigaword-100")
print("vectors:", len(g.index_to_key), " dimensions:", g.vector_size)
v = g["king"]
print("king[:8] =", np.round(v[:8], 3))
print("norm:", round(float(np.linalg.norm(v)), 3))
```

```text
vectors: 400000  dimensions: 100
trained on Wikipedia 2014 + Gigaword 5, 6 billion tokens
king[:8] = [-0.323 -0.876  0.22   0.253  0.23   0.739 -0.38  -0.353]
norm: 6.118
```

That is what a word is now: one hundred numbers, none of which means
anything on its own. The dimensions are not "royalty" and "gender" — they
are an arbitrary basis of a learned space, and asking what dimension 37
means is like asking what a principal component of some multivariate dataset
means on its own. Sometimes there is an answer; usually there is not.

```python
for w in ["king", "pump", "turkey", "python", "bank"]:
    print(f"  {w:<8} " + ", ".join(f"{a} {b:.2f}"
          for a, b in g.most_similar(w, topn=6)))
```

```text
  king     prince 0.77, queen 0.75, son 0.70, brother 0.70, monarch 0.70, throne 0.69
  pump     pumps 0.84, pumping 0.77, pumped 0.71, gasoline 0.64, fuel 0.63, petrol 0.63
  turkey   ankara 0.75, turkish 0.72, greece 0.71, syria 0.70, bulgaria 0.69, russia 0.69
  python   monty 0.69, php 0.59, perl 0.58, cleese 0.54, flipper 0.51, ruby 0.51
  bank     banks 0.81, banking 0.75, credit 0.70, investment 0.69, financial 0.68, securities 0.67
```

Three of these deserve a second look.

`turkey` returns `ankara`, `turkish`, `greece` — the country, with no trace
of the bird. `python` returns `monty` and `cleese` (the comedy troupe),
`php` and `perl` (the language), and `flipper` (the animal) — three
different meanings blended into one point. `bank` returns only the financial
sense; the river bank has been outvoted.

This is the defining limitation of a static embedding: [one vector per word
form, whatever the context]{.hl}.

Take the Turkish word *yüz*. It means *face*, it means *hundred*, and it is
the imperative *swim*. A static model gives it one row, and that row is the
weighted average of all three — a location in the space that means none of
them, sitting somewhere between anatomy, arithmetic and swimming.

Now imagine asking that vector whether a review mentioning *yüz* is about a
face cream or a hundred-lira price. It cannot answer, and no amount of
training data will change that, because the answer depends on the sentence and
the vector was fixed before the sentence existed.

Fixing exactly this is the single biggest motivation for the contextual models
in @sec-transformers.

## The famous analogy, and what it hides

You have almost certainly seen this one, and it is worth knowing what it
really shows — and what it quietly does not.

The result that made embeddings famous outside NLP:

```python
res = g.most_similar(positive=["king", "woman"], negative=["man"], topn=5)
```

```text
  queen        0.7699
  monarch      0.6843
  throne       0.6756
  daughter     0.6595
  princess     0.6521
```

$\text{king} - \text{man} + \text{woman} \approx \text{queen}$. It is a
genuinely striking result: nobody told the model about gender, and yet the
offset between `man` and `woman` is roughly the same offset as between
`king` and `queen`, so vector addition recovers it.

It is worth being explicit about why subtraction should mean anything here.
A difference of two vectors is a *direction of travel*: $\text{king} -
\text{man}$ is the instruction "whatever you have to change about `man` to
arrive at `king`." Starting from `woman` and following that same instruction
lands you at `queen` only if the instruction is the same in both places —
that is, only if the four words form a parallelogram.

And there is a reason they might. `man` and `woman` appear in near-identical
contexts apart from the handful of words that mark gender, so their vectors
end up differing mostly along whatever direction those gendered contexts
push. The same is true of `king` and `queen`. If gender is encoded as one
consistent direction rather than being tangled differently into each word,
the two offsets coincide and the arithmetic works.

That "if" is doing a lot of work, and the rest of this section is about how
often it fails.

Now the part that is usually left out. `gensim` silently excludes the three
input words from the results. Ask the question without that filter:

```python
target = g["king"] - g["man"] + g["woman"]
target /= np.linalg.norm(target)
sims = g.get_normed_vectors() @ target
for i in np.argsort(-sims)[:6]:
    print(f"  {g.index_to_key[i]:<12} {sims[i]:.4f}")
```

```text
  king         0.8552
  queen        0.7834
  monarch      0.6934
  throne       0.6833
  daughter     0.6809
  prince       0.6713
```

The nearest vector to $\text{king} - \text{man} + \text{woman}$ is
**`king`**, by a wide margin. Subtracting `man` and adding `woman` moved the
vector, but not far enough to leave `king`'s neighbourhood. The famous result
depends on a post-hoc filter that removes the true answer to the question
actually asked.

This is not a gotcha — the filter is defensible, since you rarely want an input
echoed back. But it changes what the demonstration proves, and it is worth
knowing that the method being filtered has a name. It is **3CosAdd**, and the
standard alternative, **3CosMul** [@levy2014linguistic], replaces the sum of
three cosines with a ratio, which suppresses the pull of any single input term
and gains a few points on the same question set.

The deeper objection is @linzen2016issues'. He shows that a baseline which
ignores the analogy entirely — return the nearest neighbour of `woman`, never
look at `king` or `man` — already recovers a large share of the reported
accuracy, so the headline number measures neighbourhood structure at least as
much as it measures a relation. @nissim2020fair make the complementary point
about how such results get presented. Try a few for yourself:

:::

## fastText: words made of pieces

Everything so far shares one assumption we have not questioned: that a word
is an indivisible unit with its own row in a table. Which raises a question
you already know the answer to if you read @sec-text-as-data — what happens
when a word is not in the table?

::: {#gloss-out-of-vocabulary-oov .column-margin .term-gloss}
**out-of-vocabulary (OOV)** — a word the model has no entry for, because
it was not in the training text. With a word-level vocabulary, OOV grows much
faster in morphologically rich languages; Turkish, where a stem grows dozens of
endings, makes that especially visible. [↩](#term-out-of-vocabulary-oov){.term-back}
:::

Everything so far has one vector per word form, learned only for forms seen
during training. Ask for a word the model never saw — an [out-of-vocabulary](#gloss-out-of-vocabulary-oov){#term-out-of-vocabulary-oov .term-ref}
word — and you get an exception. For English that is an annoyance. For
Turkish it is a design failure.

Here are two Wikipedia samples of comparable size, one Turkish and one
English:

```text
### corpora
  turkish   103040 lines    1458213 tokens    138578 types
  english    44079 lines    1828840 tokens     78140 types
```

Turkish produced **138,578 distinct word forms from 1.46 million tokens**;
English produced 78,140 from *more* tokens — 1.83 million. Turkish
agglutination means `ev`, `evim`, `evimde`, `evimdeki`, `evlerimizdekiler`
are five separate entries in a word-level vocabulary, each needing its own
vector, each estimated from its own sparse handful of occurrences.

```text
### vocabulary growth: new word forms per million tokens
  turkish  250k:45688  500k:73435  750k:97412  1000k:112644  1250k:126389
  english  250k:22869  500k:34016  750k:42854  1000k:52347  1250k:60178

### the tail: how much of the vocabulary is seen exactly once
  turkish   50.0% of types are hapax (69296 of 138578)
  english   46.7% of types are hapax (36503 of 78140)

### out-of-vocabulary rate: train on 90%, test on the last 10%
  turkish   7.33% of tokens unseen, 28.99% of types unseen
  english   4.72% of tokens unseen, 23.29% of types unseen
```

At one million tokens Turkish has seen 112,644 distinct forms to English's
52,347 — more than twice as many — and the curve is not flattening. Nearly
one Turkish token in fourteen in held-out text is a form the model has never
seen. Half the vocabulary occurs exactly once, which means half your
vectors are estimated from a single observation.

::: {#gloss-subword .column-margin .term-gloss}
**subword** — a piece smaller than a word. Storing pieces instead of whole
words means an unseen word can still be assembled from parts you do know. [↩](#term-subword){.term-back}
:::

fastText's answer [@bojanowski2017enriching] is to stop treating a word as
atomic. Represent it as the sum of its character n-grams — its [subwords](#gloss-subword){#term-subword .term-ref} —
plus a vector for the whole word:

$$
\mathbf{v}_{\text{word}} = \mathbf{v}_{\langle\text{word}\rangle}
+ \sum_{n\text{-grams } g} \mathbf{v}_g
$$

The sum is doing more work than it appears to. Because addition is what
combines the pieces, every n-gram vector is trained by *every* word that
contains it — `<pu` is updated by `pump`, `pumps`, `pumped`, `pumping`,
`punch` and thousands of others. A rare word is no longer estimated from its
own handful of occurrences; it is assembled from pieces that each had
plentiful data.

An unseen word still has n-grams, and those n-grams were trained on other
words. Vocabulary becomes open.

::: {.column-margin}
The trade is visible in the equation itself. A word's identity is now spread
across its spelling, so fastText cannot easily represent a word whose meaning
has nothing to do with how it is written. Sums are commutative and
indifferent; they cannot tell `<pu` "you mean something different inside
`punch` than inside `pump`."
:::

Trained on the same Turkish Wikipedia sample, word2vec and fastText behave
very differently on words the corpus never contained:

```text
### a word the corpus never saw
  kitaplarımızdaki   in word2vec vocab: False   in fastText vocab: False
    fastText still answers: kitapları 0.91, kitapların 0.91, kitaplıkları 0.90, kitaplarda 0.90
    word2vec raises: KeyError
  bilgisayarcılık    in word2vec vocab: False   in fastText vocab: False
    fastText still answers: bilgisayara 0.96, bilgisayarlı 0.96, bilgisayar 0.96, bilgisayarı 0.96
    word2vec raises: KeyError
```

The same trick handles typos, which is why fastText is a quietly popular
choice for user-generated text:

```text
  philosphy       in vocab: False
    philosophy 0.96, philosophie 0.95, philosophies 0.94, philology 0.94, philo 0.93
  governmentt     in vocab: False
    government 0.98, governments 0.94, governmental 0.93, governs 0.91, govern 0.91
```

### The price of subwords

Now the part the tutorials skip. Character n-grams buy morphology by
assuming that similar spelling implies similar meaning — and in any language
that assumption is sometimes badly wrong.

```text
### morphology: does fastText put inflected forms together?
  ft  kitap    kitapta 0.96, kitaba 0.95, kitab 0.94, kitabın 0.94, kitabı 0.93
  w2v kitap    eseri 0.81, makale 0.80, eseriyle 0.80, kitabın 0.80, kitaplar 0.79

  ft  yaz      yao 0.78, yağ 0.77, yağdı 0.77, yayoi 0.76, yay 0.75
  w2v yaz      kış 0.86, olimpiyatları 0.84, aylarında 0.83, gündönümü 0.80
```

For `kitap` (book), fastText returns inflections of `kitap`; word2vec returns
`eseri` (his/her work), `makale` (article) — *semantic* neighbours. Which one
you want depends entirely on your task.

For `yaz` (summer, and also "write") the difference is stark. word2vec
returns `kış` (winter), `olimpiyatları` (olympics), `gündönümü` (solstice) —
it has learned the season. fastText returns `yao`, `yağ` (oil), `yayoi`,
`yay` (bow) — words that share letters and nothing else. Three-character
words are mostly n-gram, so the subword signal drowns the semantic one.

```text
### the price, measured
  kitap    kitle    fastText +0.667   word2vec +0.446
```

`kitap` (book) and `kitle` (mass, crowd) are unrelated words that happen to
share three letters. fastText scores them half again as similar as word2vec
does.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**The rule to remember.** Subword models that sum character n-grams directly,
like fastText, trade semantic precision for morphological coverage. Take that
trade when your vocabulary is open and your words are long — Turkish, Finnish,
Hungarian, German compounds, chemical names, product codes, user-generated
text. Refuse it when your vocabulary is closed and short words carry the load.
BPE in @sec-text-as-data shares the engineering instinct — build rare wholes
out of frequent pieces — but the mechanism differs: BPE chooses the input
tokens, while fastText sums character n-gram embeddings into a word vector.
:::

## Documents as vectors

@sec-text-as-data classified 20 Newsgroups posts with TF-IDF. Now we have
word vectors — do they help? The question is how to produce a coordinate for a
*document* when what we have is a coordinate per word. The obvious answer is
the mean, the centroid of the word vectors in a document, which gives a
100-dimensional document vector instead of a 32,000-dimensional sparse one.

```python
def average(docs):
    out = np.zeros((len(docs), g.vector_size), dtype=np.float32)
    for i, d in enumerate(docs):
        vs = [g[w] for w in d if w in g.key_to_index]
        if vs:
            out[i] = np.mean(vs, axis=0)
    return out
```

A step up from the plain mean is to weight it by IDF:

$$
v_d = \frac{\sum_{w \in d} \mathrm{idf}(w)\, v_w}{\sum_{w \in d} \mathrm{idf}(w)}
$$

The idea from @sec-text-as-data carries over: let words that appear in every
document steer the average less. That variant appears in the table below as
`idf-weighted averaged glove`.

doc2vec [@le2014distributed] does something less naive: it learns a vector
per *document* by the same negative-sampling trick, treating the document id
as an extra context. It comes in two flavours:

| Variant | Input | Predicts |
|---|---|---|
| **PV-DM** | document vector + context words | the target word |
| **PV-DBOW** | the document vector alone | words sampled from the document |

: The two doc2vec variants {tbl-colwidths="[22,44,34]"}

Loosely, they are the CBOW and skip-gram of the document world — the
input–output columns show they are not literally the same models.

::: {.column-margin}
Which flavour wins is not settled by the original paper. @le2014distributed
recommend PV-DM; @lau2016empirical re-ran both carefully and found PV-DBOW at
least as strong and much cheaper, which is why `gensim`'s defaults and most
later work follow it. doc2vec is also the field's best-known reproducibility
case: the paper's headline IMDB error rate was not independently reproduced for
years, and the gap turned out to be hyperparameters and training length rather
than the architecture. Read it as a cautionary tale about single-number claims.
:::
